'''Kōichirō Nishikawa''' ({{langx|ja|西川 公一郎}}, born 1949 - November 28, 2018) was a Japanese elementary particle physicist, known for contributions to [[neutrino]] physics. He was professor emeritus of the [[KEK]] high-energy physics laboratory and [[University of Kyoto|Kyōto University]].

Nishikawa graduated from Kyōto University in 1971 and completed his doctorate at [[Northwestern University|Northwestern]] in 1980 working with {{ill|David Buchholz (physicist)|qid=Q56676649|lt=David Buchholz}}. After working at the [[University of Chicago]], [[State University of New York]], and [[University of Tokyo|Tōkyō University]], he combined positions at KEK and Kyōto University, eventually becoming director of the Institute for Particle and Nuclear physics at the KEK laboratory and deputy director of the [[J-PARC]] proton accelerator facility.<ref name="INSPIRE-HEP">{{cite web | title=Nishikawa, Koichiro - Profile | website=INSPIRE-HEP | url=https://inspirehep.net/author/profile/K.Nishikawa.1 | access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref><ref name="KEK2011">{{cite journal| title= 2011 at KEK, Annual Report| publisher=KEK|citeseerx = 10.1.1.670.8237}}</ref>

Nishikawa's most notable achievements were as founder and leader of the [[K2K]] and [[T2K]] experiments.<ref name="J-PARC">{{cite web | title=J-PARC News in English 2015 | website=J-PARC | url=https://j-parc.jp/en/news/2015/J-PARC_News-e1511.html | access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref> K2K, which ran from 1999 until 2005, used the [[Super Kamiokande]] detector in [[Kamioka]] to measure a controlled beam of neutrinos emitted by the KEK proton synchrotron. The K2K team verified with greater accuracy the neutrino oscillations observed in atmospheric neutrinos by the Super Kamiokande experiment.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://cerncourier.com/synthetic-neutrinos-appear-to-disappear/| title=Synthetic neutrinos appear to disappear| work=CERN Courier| date=17 October 2000| access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref> The T2K experiment, which began in 2010 as a successor to K2K, used neutrino beams from the [[J-PARC]] proton accelerator with the Super Kamiokande detector to observe neutrino oscillations with specific start and end flavors, thereby measuring the parameters of this flavor-switching behavior.<ref name="Parke">{{cite magazine | last=Parke | first=Stephen J. | title=Viewpoint: A new neutrino oscillation | magazine=Physics | volume=4 | date=18 July 2011 | doi=10.1103/Physics.4.57 | url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v4/57 | access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref>

In 2016, Nishikawa and the [[K2K]] and [[T2K]] groups received the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] together with other neutrino research collaborations.<ref name="Breakthrough Prize 2016">{{cite web | title=Breakthrough Prize – Fundamental Physics Breakthrough Prize Laureates – Koichiro Nishikawa and the K2K and T2K Collaboration | website=Breakthrough Prize | date=1 October 2016 | url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/1/L155 | access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Nishina Memorial Prize]] in 2005,<ref name="nishina">{{cite web | title=Nishina Memorial Prize| website=nishina-mf.or.jp| date=18 December 2013| url=http://www.nishina-mf.or.jp/NishinaMemorialPrize-E.html| access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref> and the [[Bruno Pontecorvo Prize]] in 2016.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://t2k-experiment.org/2017/03/koichiro-nishikawa-wins-2016-pontecorvo-prize/| title=Koichiro Nishikawa wins 2016 Pontecorvo Prize| date=1 March 2017| website=t2k-experiment.org| access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref> He also received the 1998 [[Asahi Prize]] as part of the [[Super-Kamiokande]] experiment that discovered the mass of neutrinos.<ref name="Asahi">{{cite web | author=The Asahi Shimbun Company | title=The Asahi Prize - English Information | website=The Asahi Shimbun Company | url=https://www.asahi.com/shimbun/award/asahi/english.html | access-date=20 September 2018}}</ref>
